passages.title: Direct or diplomatic?
passages.text: In some cultures, people say exactly what they mean. In others, the most important part of a message is what is left unsaid. A manager from one tradition may consider it perfectly normal to tell a colleague that a report is poor, whereas a colleague from another might express the same view by asking whether the report could be developed further. Neither style is better than the other, but misunderstandings arise when people from different traditions work together. To someone used to directness, a tactful comment can seem like beating around the bush; to someone used to subtlety, a blunt remark can sound rude, even aggressive. Register adds another layer of complexity. The same request can be made in very different ways: "Send me the file" is acceptable between close colleagues, but "Would you mind sending me the file?" is safer with a client, and "I would be grateful if you could forward the document" belongs in a formal letter. Learners of English often master grammar long before they master these social rules. What experienced communicators do is read between the lines, notice how others speak and adapt their own style accordingly.

passages.title: The case for plain language
passages.text: Why do so many official documents seem designed to be misunderstood? Part of the answer lies in jargon. Every profession develops its own vocabulary, and within a group of experts, technical terms allow people to communicate quickly and precisely. The problem arises when the same language is used with people outside that group. A patient who is told that a test result is "unremarkable" may assume the worst, when in fact it means that nothing is wrong. Another problem is the excessive use of nominalization. A sentence such as "The implementation of the reduction of costs will be the responsibility of the department" is grammatically correct, yet it hides who is supposed to do what. "The department will cut costs" says the same thing in five words. Campaigners for plain language argue that clarity is not the same as simplification. Complex ideas can be expressed clearly, and readers should not need a dictionary to understand a letter from their bank. Some governments now require public documents to be tested on ordinary readers before they are published. If you cannot get your point across to a non-expert, the argument goes, perhaps the point itself is not as clear as you think.

points: En un correo formal se pide de forma indirecta: «I would be grateful if you could…».
«blunt» es demasiado directo, casi brusco; «tactful», con tacto.
«beat around the bush» es andarse con rodeos; «read between the lines», leer entre líneas.
El registro también cambia las palabras: «buy» → «purchase», «ask for» → «request».

examples.en: I would be grateful if you could send me the document.
examples.es: Le agradecería que me enviara el documento.

examples.en: Stop beating around the bush and tell me what happened.

mistake.wrong: I want that you send me the document.
mistake.right: I would be grateful if you could send me the document.
mistake.note: “Quiero que…” no se dice con «want that», y en un correo formal suena brusco.

points: Nominalizar es convertir verbos en sustantivos: «decide» → «decision», «develop» → «development».
Es típico del inglés formal: «the introduction of the rules» en vez de «when they introduced the rules».
Pero el exceso cansa: «plain language» es escribir claro, sin «jargon» (jerga técnica).
«get your point across» es lograr que te entiendan.

examples.en: The implementation of the new rules has been delayed.
examples.es: La aplicación de las nuevas normas se ha retrasado.

examples.en: She struggled to get her point across in English.
examples.es: Le costó hacerse entender en inglés.

mistake.wrong: The implement of the rules was delayed.
mistake.right: The implementation of the rules was delayed.
mistake.note: Después de «the» va un sustantivo: «implementation», no el verbo «implement».
